paragraphs: And so Mitya sat staring wildly at the people around him, not taking in what was said to him. Suddenly he jumped up, threw up his hands and shouted:
“I’m not guilty! I’m not guilty of that blood! I’m not guilty of my father’s blood.... I meant to kill him. But I’m not guilty. Not I.”
But he had barely said it when Grushenka rushed out from behind the curtain and threw herself down at the police captain’s feet.

“It was my fault! Mine! My wickedness!” she cried in a heartbreaking voice, drenched in tears, holding out her clasped hands to them. “He did it because of me. I tortured him and drove him to it. In my wickedness I tortured that poor old man who’s dead, too, and brought him to this! It’s my fault, mine first, mine most, my fault!”

“Yes, it’s your fault! You’re the chief criminal! You fury! You harlot! You’re the most to blame!” shouted the police captain, shaking his fist at her. But he was quickly and firmly stopped. The prosecutor simply grabbed hold of him.
“This is completely out of order, Mihail Makarovitch!” he cried. “You’re plainly obstructing the inquiry.... You’re ruining the case....” He was almost gasping.
“Follow the proper procedure! Follow the proper procedure!” cried Nikolay Parfenovitch, who was in a fearful state of excitement too. “Otherwise it’s absolutely impossible!...”
“Judge us together!” Grushenka cried frantically, still on her knees. “Punish us together. I’ll go with him now, even if it’s to death!”

“Grusha, my life, my blood, my holy one!” Mitya fell on his knees beside her and held her tight in his arms. “Don’t believe her,” he cried. “She’s not guilty of anything, not of any blood, of anything!”

He remembered afterwards that several men dragged him away from her by force, that she was led out, and that when he came to himself he was sitting at the table. Beside him and behind him stood the men with the metal plates. Across the table sat Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, who kept urging him to drink a little water from a glass on the table.

“It will refresh you, it will calm you. Be calm, don’t be frightened,” he added, extremely politely. Mitya (he remembered it afterwards) suddenly became intensely interested in the lawyer’s big rings, one with an amethyst and another with a clear, bright yellow stone of great brilliance. And long afterwards he remembered with wonder how those rings had held his attention through all those terrible hours of questioning. He simply could not tear himself away from them and dismiss them as things that had nothing to do with his situation. On Mitya’s left, in the place where Maximov had been sitting at the start of the evening, the prosecutor now sat. On Mitya’s right, where Grushenka had been, was a rosy-cheeked young man in a sort of shabby hunting jacket, with ink and paper in front of him. This was the investigating lawyer’s secretary, whom he had brought with him. The police captain was now standing by the window at the far end of the room, next to Kalganov, who was sitting there.
“Drink some water,” said the investigating lawyer softly, for the tenth time.
“I have drunk it, gentlemen, I have ... but ... come, gentlemen, crush me, punish me, decide my fate!” cried Mitya, staring at the investigating lawyer with terribly fixed, wide-open eyes.
“So you firmly declare that you are not guilty of the death of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch?” asked the investigating lawyer, softly but insistently.

“I am not guilty. I am guilty of the blood of another old man, but not of my father’s. And I weep for it! I killed him, I killed the old man and knocked him down.... But it’s hard to have to answer for that murder with another one, a terrible murder that I’m not guilty of.... It’s a terrible accusation, gentlemen, a knock-down blow. But who killed my father, who killed him? Who can have killed him if I didn’t? It’s amazing, extraordinary, impossible.”
“Yes, who can have killed him?” the investigating lawyer was beginning, but Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, glanced at him and spoke to Mitya.

“You need not worry about the old servant, Grigory Vassilyevitch. He is alive and has recovered. According to his own evidence and yours, you struck him terrible blows, and yet there seems to be no doubt that he will live, or so the doctor says, at least.”

“Alive? He’s alive?” cried Mitya, throwing up his hands. His face beamed. “Lord, I thank You for the miracle You have worked for me, a sinner and evildoer. That’s the answer to my prayer. I’ve been praying all night.” And he crossed himself three times. He was almost breathless.
“So from this Grigory we have received such important evidence concerning you, that—” The prosecutor would have gone on, but Mitya suddenly jumped up from his chair.
“One minute, gentlemen, for God’s sake, one minute; I’ll run to her—”
“Excuse me, at this moment it’s quite impossible,” Nikolay Parfenovitch almost shrieked. He, too, leapt to his feet. The men with the metal plates seized Mitya, but he sat down of his own accord....

“Gentlemen, what a pity! I wanted to see her for one minute only. I wanted to tell her that it has been washed away, it’s gone, that blood that weighed on my heart all night, and that I’m not a murderer now! Gentlemen, she is my betrothed!” he said, ecstatic and reverent, looking round at them all. “Oh, thank you, gentlemen! Oh, in one minute you have given me new life, a new heart!... That old man used to carry me in his arms, gentlemen. He used to wash me in the tub when I was a baby of three, abandoned by everyone. He was like a father to me!...”
“And so you—” the investigating lawyer began.

“Allow me, gentlemen, allow me one minute more,” Mitya broke in, putting his elbows on the table and covering his face with his hands. “Give me a moment to think, let me breathe, gentlemen. All this is horribly upsetting, horribly. A man is not a drum, gentlemen!”
“Drink a little more water,” murmured Nikolay Parfenovitch.

Mitya took his hands from his face and laughed. His eyes were full of confidence. In a moment he seemed completely transformed. His whole manner had changed. He was once more the equal of these men, all of whom he knew, as though they had all met the day before, when nothing had happened, at some social gathering. We may note in passing that when Mitya first arrived in town, the police captain had made him very welcome. Later, especially during the last month, Mitya had hardly called at all. When the police captain met him in the street, for instance, Mitya had noticed that he frowned and only bowed out of politeness. His acquaintance with the prosecutor was less close. He did sometimes pay polite visits to the prosecutor’s wife, a nervous and fanciful lady, without quite knowing why. She always received him graciously and, for some reason, had taken an interest in him right up to the end. He had not had time to get to know the investigating lawyer, though he had met him and talked to him twice, each time about the fair sex.

“You’re a most skillful lawyer, I see, Nikolay Parfenovitch,” cried Mitya, laughing gaily. “But I can help you now. Oh, gentlemen, I feel like a new man, and don’t be offended that I speak to you so simply and directly. I’m a bit drunk, too, I’ll tell you that frankly. I believe I’ve had the honor and pleasure of meeting you, Nikolay Parfenovitch, at my kinsman Miüsov’s. Gentlemen, gentlemen, I don’t pretend to be on equal terms with you. I understand, of course, in what character I’m sitting before you. Oh, of course, there’s a horrible suspicion ... hanging over me ... if Grigory has given evidence.... A horrible suspicion! It’s awful, awful, I understand that! But to business, gentlemen. I’m ready, and we’ll make an end of it in one moment. Because, listen, listen, gentlemen! Since I know I’m innocent, we can put an end to it in a minute. Can’t we? Can’t we?”
Mitya spoke a great deal and very fast, nervously and gushingly, as though he honestly took his listeners to be his best friends.

“So for the present we will write down that you flatly deny the charge brought against you,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch impressively. Bending down to the secretary, he dictated to him in an undertone what to write.

“Write it down? You want to write that down? Well, write it. I consent, I give my full consent, gentlemen, only ... do you see?... Wait, wait, write this. Of disorderly conduct I am guilty, of violence to a poor old man I am guilty. And there is something else at the bottom of my heart that I’m guilty of, too—but that you needn’t write down” (he turned suddenly to the secretary). “That’s my personal life, gentlemen, that doesn’t concern you, the bottom of my heart, that’s to say.... But of the murder of my old father I’m not guilty. That’s a wild idea. It’s quite a wild idea!... I’ll prove it to you, and you’ll be convinced at once.... You’ll laugh, gentlemen. You’ll laugh at your own suspicion!...”

“Be calm, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said the investigating lawyer, evidently trying to ease Mitya’s excitement with his own composure. “Before we go on with our inquiry, I should like, if you are willing to answer, to hear you confirm that you disliked your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and that you were in constant quarrels with him. Here, at least, a quarter of an hour ago, you exclaimed that you wanted to kill him: ‘I didn’t kill him,’ you said, ‘but I wanted to kill him.’”
“Did I shout that? Ach, that may be so, gentlemen! Yes, unfortunately, I did want to kill him ... many times I wanted to ... unfortunately, unfortunately!”
“You wanted to. Would you be willing to explain exactly what reasons led you to such hatred of your parent?”

“What is there to explain, gentlemen?” Mitya shrugged sullenly, looking down. “I’ve never hidden my feelings. All the town knows about it—everyone in the tavern knows. Only recently I declared them in Father Zossima’s cell.... And the very same day, in the evening, I beat my father. I nearly killed him, and I swore in front of witnesses that I’d come back and kill him.... Oh, a thousand witnesses! I’ve been shouting it out for the last month, anyone can tell you that!... The fact stares you in the face, it speaks for itself, it cries out, but feelings, gentlemen, feelings are another matter. You see, gentlemen”—Mitya frowned—“it seems to me that you’ve no right to question me about feelings. I know you’re bound by your office, I quite understand that, but that’s my affair, my private, intimate affair, and yet ... since I haven’t hidden my feelings in the past ... in the tavern, for instance, I’ve talked to everyone, so ... so I won’t make a secret of it now. You see, I understand, gentlemen, that there are terrible facts against me in this business. I told everyone I’d kill him, and now, all of a sudden, he’s been killed. So it must have been me! Ha ha! I can make allowances for you, gentlemen, I really can. I’m stunned myself, for who can have murdered him, if not I? That’s what it comes to, isn’t it? If not I, who can it be, who? Gentlemen, I want to know, I insist on knowing!” he exclaimed suddenly. “Where was he murdered? How was he murdered? How, and with what? Tell me,” he asked quickly, looking at the two lawyers.
